p.x:
Last month, there was a big flood in a village near my town. Many families lost their homes and their food. Our teacher said, "They need our help."
So we brought rice, water and clothes to school. We also walked around the market with a bucket to collect money. People were very kind and helpful. In one day, we collected 8,000 baht!
We sent everything to the village. A week later, the village head sent us a letter. "We are so thankful," he wrote. "Your gifts give us hope." I felt very happy that we could help.

p.t: How to Raise Money for Charity
p.x:
Do you want to make a difference? Raising money for charity can be easy and fun. Here are some ideas.
A bake sale is popular in schools: students make cakes and sell them at a stall. You can also organise a sponsored walk, where friends and family promise to give money for every kilometre you walk. A raffle, where people buy tickets to win a prize, is another good way to raise money at a fundraiser.
Before you start, choose a charity. Some charities help orphans or refugees, while others provide clean water or fight poverty. Make leaflets to explain why the cause is important.
Many people also volunteer or donate regularly as a way to give back to society. Even small amounts help. Large organisations often hold a gala dinner for rich donors, and some NGOs receive a grant from the government. In disaster relief, quick help saves lives. Experts say a recurring monthly donation is more useful than one large gift, because charities can plan ahead. Donors sometimes pledge large sums for humanitarian emergencies. Many charitable groups also work on sanitation, building toilets to stop disease. Some countries give foreign aid to poorer nations. Whatever you choose, your generosity can change lives.

Every year, governments, organisations and individuals give hundreds of billions of dollars to help people in need. Yet economists continue to debate a fundamental question: does aid actually work?
Supporters point to remarkable achievements. International programmes have helped to eliminate smallpox, sharply reduce child deaths and bring education to millions. Philanthropy by wealthy individuals and foundations, some with endowments worth billions, has funded vaccines and research that governments could not afford. In many countries, donations are tax-deductible, encouraging further giving, and schemes that offer matched funding can double the impact of individual gifts.
Critics, however, argue that some aid creates dependency, discouraging local governments and businesses from developing their own solutions. Others point out that money is sometimes lost to corruption or spent on projects that do not reflect local needs. A charity's trustees and its patron may be prominent public figures, but celebrity support does not guarantee effectiveness.
In response, many organisations have shifted their focus towards sustainable development and empowerment, helping communities build long-term independence rather than simply providing goods. Microfinance, which offers small loans to entrepreneurs who cannot access banks, became famous for this approach, although its results have been mixed. An anonymous benefactor who funds a local school run by the community may achieve more than a large project imposed from outside. The most effective aid, many experts now agree, listens to the people it is meant to help.
